content: Amoxicillin, also known as amoxycillin, is a moderate-spectrum β-lactam antibiotic that is commonly used to treat bacterial infections caused by susceptible microorganisms. It is often preferred within its class due to its superior absorption when administered orally compared to other β-lactam antibiotics. However, amoxicillin is vulnerable to degradation by β-lactamase enzymes produced by certain bacteria. To counteract this, it is frequently combined with clavulanic acid, a β-lactamase inhibitor, to enhance its efficacy. Amoxicillin was originally developed by Beecham in 1972 and is now marketed by GlaxoSmithKline under the trade name Amoxil. The mechanism of action of amoxicillin involves the inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis. Specifically, it prevents the cross-linking of peptidoglycan polymer chains, which are essential structural components of the cell walls in Gram-positive bacteria. Amoxicillin exhibits activity against a range of microorganisms. Among Gram-positive bacteria, it is effective against Streptococcus species, penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, non-β-lactamase-producing Staphylococcus species, and Enterococcus faecalis. For Gram-negative bacteria, it is active against non-β-lactamase-producing strains of Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Neisseria meningitidis, Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis, and Salmonella species. However, amoxicillin is ineffective against penicillinase-producing organisms, including penicillinase-producing Staphylococcus species, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and Haemophilus influenzae. It is also resistant to all strains of Pseudomonas species, Klebsiella species, Enterobacter species, indole-positive Proteus species, Serratia marcescens, and Citrobacter species. The prevalence of β-lactamase-producing resistant organisms, such as Escherichia coli, is increasing. In pediatric cases, doubling the standard dose of amoxicillin has been shown to eradicate intermediately resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae in certain infections. Amoxicillin is available in various formulations. The trihydrate form is used for oral administration in capsules, tablets, or syrup, while the sodium salt form is used for intravenous administration. It is one of the most commonly prescribed antibiotics for children and has three ionizable groups. When combined with clavulanic acid (as potassium clavulanate), amoxicillin's spectrum of activity is broadened to include additional Gram-negative organisms. This combination also helps overcome bacterial resistance mediated by β-lactamase production. The formulation is commonly referred to as Co-amoxiclav or by proprietary names such as Augmentin, Amoksiklav, and Clamoxyl. The side effects of amoxicillin are similar to those of other β-lactam antibiotics. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, and fatigue. Allergic reactions to amoxicillin can occur suddenly and may be severe, requiring immediate medical attention. Symptoms of an allergic reaction may include changes in mental state, an intensely itchy skin rash (often starting at the fingertips or groin and spreading rapidly), fever, nausea, and vomiting. Any unusual symptoms should be taken seriously and evaluated promptly. Since the patent for amoxicillin has expired, it is now marketed under numerous trade names worldwide, including Actimoxi, Amoxil, Amoxiclav Sandoz, Augmentin, Curam, Duomox, Ospamox, Trimox, and Zimox, among many others.
